title_en: Find a fraction on a line
question_en: How can a fraction name a place between 0 and 1?
idea_en: The denominator counts equal spaces in one whole; the numerator counts spaces from 0.
steps_en: Find the whole stretch from 0 to 1.
Count its equal spaces to find the denominator.
Count spaces from 0 to the point to find the numerator.

example_en.prompt: What fraction is at point P?
steps: The whole has 5 equal spaces.
Point P is 3 spaces from 0.
That is 3 out of 5 equal spaces: 3/5.

remember_en: Count the spaces, not the tick marks. Starting at 0 is not a step.

connects_to.label_en: Place likelihood on a zero-to-one scale

question_en: How do I compare fractions with the same denominator?
idea_en: For the same-sized whole, more parts of the same size make a greater fraction.
steps_en: Check that the wholes match and the denominators are the same.
Compare the numerators: they count the parts.
Choose <, > or = to show the relationship.

steps: Both fractions count parts of a whole split into 8 equal spaces.
5/8 is further to the right on this line.

remember_en: Compare the same-sized whole. The open side of < or > faces the greater amount.

question_en: Why does the denominator stay the same when I add these fractions?
idea_en: We join the counts of equal-sized parts, while the size of each part stays the same.
steps_en: Use the same whole and check that the denominators match.
Add the numerators to count all the parts.
Keep the denominator because each part is still the same size.

steps: The whole is split into 8 equal parts.
Join 2 parts and 3 more parts: 2 + 3 = 5 parts.
The parts are still eighths, so the sum is 5/8.

remember_en: Adding parts does not cut each part into smaller pieces.

question_en: How do I subtract fractions without changing the whole?
idea_en: Take away a count of equal-sized parts, but keep the original whole as your unit.
steps_en: Start with the first number of equal parts.
Take away the second number of parts.
Keep the denominator: the original part size has not changed.

steps: Start with 7 tenths of the original whole.
Take away 3 tenths: 7 - 3 = 4 tenths remain.
The remaining fraction is 4/10.

remember_en: The pieces left are not a new whole. Keep the original whole in mind.

question_en: What does one sixth of an amount mean?
idea_en: The denominator tells us how many equal groups make the whole; one sixth is one of six groups.
steps_en: Find the whole amount.
Use the denominator to decide how many equal groups to make.
Share the whole equally, then take one group.

steps: The 6 in 1/6 means 6 equal groups, not 6 counters per group.
Share the whole: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 counters in each group.
Take one group. Check: 7 × 6 = 42.

remember_en: Multiply the amount in one group by the denominator. You should get the whole amount back.

title_en: Build the whole from one part
question_en: How can one known equal part help me find the whole?
idea_en: Repeat the known part as many times as the denominator says to build the whole.
steps_en: Find the amount in one equal part.
Read the denominator to find how many parts make the whole.
Multiply one part by the number of equal parts.

example_en.prompt: 1/6 of a ribbon is 7 cm. How long is the whole ribbon?
steps: The 7 cm labels one part, not the whole ribbon.
Build 6 equal parts: 7 × 6 = 42 cm.
Check one part again: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 cm.

remember_en: Ask whether the known amount is one part or the whole before choosing an operation.

connects_to.label_en: Find the whole from a non-unit fraction

question_en: How do I find several equal parts of an amount?
idea_en: Find one equal part first, then combine as many parts as the numerator asks for.
steps_en: Use the denominator to split the whole into equal parts.
Divide the whole by the denominator to find one part.
Multiply one part by the numerator to find the parts you want.

example_en.prompt: 3/5 of 30 marbles are blue. How many are blue?
steps: Split 30 marbles into 5 equal parts: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 per part.
The numerator asks for 3 parts: 6 × 3 = 18.
The highlighted 3 parts contain 18 blue marbles.

remember_en: The bottom number splits the whole. The top number chooses how many parts.

title_en: Build the whole from several parts
question_en: How do I find the whole when I know the amount in several parts?
idea_en: The known amount covers several equal parts; find one part before rebuilding the whole.
steps_en: The numerator tells you how many parts have a known total.
Divide that known total by the numerator to find one part.
Multiply one part by the denominator to build the whole.

example_en.prompt: 3/5 of a ribbon is 18 cm. How long is the whole ribbon?
steps: The 18 cm covers 3 parts together, not one part.
Find one part: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 cm.
Build all 5 parts: 6 × 5 = 30 cm.

remember_en: Label what you know first: the whole, one part, or several parts.
